canonical_claim: S37 is commissioned to test multi-disk policies containing local and CA disks, including mixed-disk merges and atomic restart recovery during policy moves.

Unversioned RustFS overwrites of objects larger than 128 KiB leak the previous data directory; scanner reclamation found zero files after more than two hours, and LIST operations timed out around 600,000 files. Additionally, The refined F2 root cause is RustFS issue `rustfs#3231`: overwriting objects larger than 128 KiB in an unversioned bucket leaks prior data directories, and metacache walks then time out and produce LIST storms and 503s.

The clamped-shard incident was caused by RustFS false 404s on `HEAD` during a `rustfs#3231` metacache storm; the false 404s produced clamps, and clamp suppression prevented graduation over unfolded events until the storm ended.

Local or NFS multi-server pools can start with per-process conditional-operation emulation that violates CAS and GC invariants, because the implementation logs an INFO message and continues. Additionally, The local or NFS backend is not safe for racy multi-writer put-if-absent use because it lacks the atomicity guarantees provided by S3 conditional PUTs.

Unknown GCS bucket-versioning state fails open: inability to determine versioning only logs and continues, although enabled versioning archives generations and prevents GC from reclaiming storage.; Bucket versioning and versioning-suspended mode are rejected for the CA prefix because delete markers break the one-live-object model. Additionally, A generation-token store forces single-part conditional uploads and rejects versioned GCS buckets because exact-token delete would archive rather than reclaim the old generation. Additionally, CAS backup requires bucket versioning to be off; versioning-suspended buckets are rejected as well. Additionally, A generation-dialect GCS bucket with object versioning enabled is rejected with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` because token-exact DELETE archives a noncurrent generation instead of reclaiming storage. Additionally, `isBucketVersioningEnabled` returns `std::nullopt` when the bucket versioning status is unknown or not applicable; the CAS probe fails closed when a generation-dialect storage explicitly reports versioning enabled. Additionally, A GCS versioned bucket is rejected even though per-operation conditional checks may pass, because versioning turns token-exact deletion into archival and silently prevents storage reclamation. Additionally, Review finding №17 leaves unknown GCS bucket versioning as an explicit-WARNING tradeoff: confirmed `Enabled` fails, but an unverifiable check proceeds to avoid overly aggressive mount refusal.

RustFS failed the LIST-consistency passport by omitting keys that had been durable for 19 seconds, so conservative probe-always behavior remains the default. Additionally, The fail-close default for LIST trust is probe-always, and RustFS currently fails the proposed passport by measurement. Additionally, A RustFS ref-log enumeration omitted durable predecessor keys `0x1430c` and `0x1430d` while returning later `0x1430e`; exact-key `GET` and `HEAD` still reported the omitted objects present.; The fix must tolerate an object store that returns inconsistent `LIST` results; RustFS demonstrated inconsistency and AWS S3 was untested at the time of the debt record.

GC discovery requires strong LIST consistency: an object PUT before the LIST boundary must appear in the discovery result. Additionally, The D1 plan treats read-your-writes enumeration from `LIST(cas/refs/)` as load-bearing; a backend without that consistency is unsupported and must fail closed. Additionally, D1 requires strongly consistent LIST with read-your-writes enumeration; S3 is stated to provide it, while an unsupported backend must be documented and fail closed rather than use a silent fallback. Additionally, The required read-after-write visibility contract applies to both ref-log `LIST` and canonical ordering: a backend without visibility or ordering cannot enable the format and may not substitute an unbounded in-memory sort. Additionally, The LIST-consistency probe in `Cas::Probe` is load-bearing before LIST-derived discovery can be trusted on a store, because S3 LIST may omit a just-PUT key. Additionally, The root-local part-manifest model assumes backend LIST consistency for shard discovery; the implementation must confirm strongly consistent LIST semantics per backend. Additionally, The shard-incarnation model assumes discovery equals present shards and therefore assumes strongly consistent backend LIST semantics. Additionally, The D1 design treats LIST consistency as load-bearing and requires RustFS and `InMemoryBackend` semantics to be confirmed; an unsupported backend must remain fail-closed.; Tail under-reporting of a completed write is illegal on a compliant store under the read-after-write clause and is the only LIST property a per-backend trust mode may rely on.

CA requires server-enforced conditional PUT, COPY, and DELETE semantics, a write-time incarnation token, bucket versioning off, and strong LIST consistency.; The backend must provide read-after-write visibility, conditional create via `putIfAbsent`, conditional overwrite via `casPut` or `putOverwrite`, exact-token deletion via `deleteExact`, no versioning or delete markers, and token-to-content stability.; The CAS ref design relies on exact-GET and token-CAS backend semantics; a backend that violates those primitives is outside the admissible pool contract and must fail its capability probe.

The RustFS CA stateless job is required because MinIO OSS lacks the enforced conditional deletes needed by the incarnation pool's fail-closed probe. Additionally, S3-native staging's real conditional-write/server-side-copy promote path is exercised only via RustFS in CI and integration tests, because MinIO OSS lacks the enforced conditional deletes the capability probe requires; the in-process gtest only covers the local-staging path. Additionally, Current integration tests use MinIO, but the production gate requires RustFS coverage because production S3-compatible backends enforce conditional PUT. Additionally, The CA integration harness uses RustFS rather than MinIO because the CAS tests require conditional-PUT semantics that MinIO did not enforce in the observed setup.; The backend capability probe runs at every writable mount and refuses an object store that does not enforce the CAS conditions. Additionally, The CAS capability probe requires an object store that enforces conditional operations, including wrong-token DELETE returning 412; the suite therefore uses RustFS `1.0.0-beta.8`, not MinIO.

AWS S3 conforms to the CAS backend requirements: capability probing observes honest 412 responses for wrong-token conditional operations, two-phase reclaim deletes objects physically, and fsck remains clean through more than 28 GC rounds.

The GCS S3-compatible endpoint silently ignores `If-None-Match`, `If-Match` overwrite, and `If-Match` delete preconditions; notably, a wrong-ETag DELETE can delete the object. Additionally, Live GCS probes found that the S3-compatible surface silently ignores `If-None-Match` and `If-Match` on PUT and DELETE, so the CAS capability probe refuses that mode with exit 48.

A strongly consistent meta GET is a pool requirement because the writer must not adopt a body whose current incarnation has already been condemned.; The one-GET meta-adopt path requires a backend with strong read-after-write consistency; the plan identifies S3 since 2020 and RustFS as satisfying that requirement.
The supported platform wording for CAS object storage is: AWS and GCP work, Azure probably works, and other S3-compatible stores require atomic or conditional operations such as `If-None-Match`.

Predecessor omission below a correct LIST tail is legal on contract-compliant S3 for writes concurrent with a paginated enumeration because S3 provides no snapshot contract for keys landing during the walk.

The pointer CAS design is supported by RustFS/AWS and S3-compatible GCS plus EmulatedSingleProcess, but Azure or non-S3 native object storage is not an admitted writable CAS backend under the current single-attempt retry profile

If a backend advertises `supportsListTokens`, every listed item should provide a token compatible with `deleteExact` and matching `head`; otherwise the capability must distinguish no tokens from head-only tokens.

Review finding №15 leaves shared local-pool startup behavior as a design decision because single-server ownership cannot be proved inside the process, and changing INFO to WARNING would break default CA-over-local tests.
A CAS bucket passport can be operator attestation per bucket, continuous verification with auto-revocation, or both; trust is a runtime property of a bucket rather than a backend type string.
GOOG4-HMAC-SHA256 over the GCS XML endpoint enforced the full 12/12 conditional probe battery, showing that the CAS incompatibility is a signing-dialect problem rather than an API-migration problem.
With versioning disabled, CAS cannot use S3 CRR/SRR, AWS Backup for S3, S3 Object Lock, or Azure soft-delete and blob-versioning facilities that require versioning.
Garage was rejected as a CAS backend because it silently ignores conditional operations such as `If-None-Match`, while RustFS passed the conditional-write battery.

The CI RustFS setup required a downloaded arch-aware beta.9 binary because `start_rustfs` expected `ci/tmp/rustfs`; beta.9 passed the conditional-operation probes where a second `If-None-Match: *` PUT and a wrong-etag DELETE return 412.
A CA disk without an explicit scratch path creates `<data-path>/disks/<name>/cas_scratch/` at startup, and the parent `disks/` directory must be writable by the server user.

On generation-token backends, `gcs_max_conditional_put_bytes` defaults to 1 GiB and conditional writes larger than that are rejected with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; the limit is irrelevant to ETag-based AWS S3 backends.
Azure real-store GC validation remained the last leg of the real-S3 reclaim release gate after AWS and GCS validation.

A mount-time `Cas::Probe` should write a known key set, enumerate it, and refuse LIST-derived discovery on a backend that cannot return the set; the existing `list_consistency_hammer.py` is not this capability probe.

The factory configuration key gcs_max_conditional_put_bytes maps to the member gc_max_conditional_put_bytes_, dropping the s and making the member name misleading.; Risk register #11 (Medium, confirmed): a config-key/member naming trap exists where `gcs_max_conditional_put_bytes` is stored in a member named `gc_max_conditional_put_bytes_` (reads as garbage-collection, `MetadataStorageFactory.cpp:291` vs `.h:286`), and `root_shards` has a constructor default of 8 (`.h:73`) vs a factory default of 32 (`:251`) — a creation-time-only constant, so this is a real unit-vs-production divergence risk. Suggested action: rename the member; align the defaults.; `registerContentAddressedMetadataStorage` must use the `gcs_max_conditional_put_bytes_` member name, throw `DB::Exception` with `NO_ELEMENTS_IN_CONFIG` when `server_root_id` is missing, and reconcile the `cas_` prefix on part-folder-cache keys.

The metadata factory silently overrode the intended 32 `root_shards` with a default of 8; changing the factory default to 32 was verified live with shard indexes up to 27. Additionally, For `ContentAddressedMetadataStorage`, the ctor default for `root_shards_` is 8 while the factory's config default is 32; a pool minted via the ctor default (e.g. in a unit test bypassing the factory) is stuck at fanout 8 because `root_shards` is creation-time-only.; The content_addressed factory defaults include gc_enabled=true, gc_interval_sec=60, root_shards=32, blob_hash=cityhash128, dedup_cache_bytes=64 MiB, and dedup_head_first_min_bytes=1 MiB. Additionally, The shipped factory default for `root_shards` is 32.; Lazy journal trim compacts a shard when trimmable events reach `gc_trim_min_events` (default 256, with 0 meaning eager) or encoded body size reaches `gc_trim_body_soft_limit` (default 8 MiB). Additionally, The validated CAS defaults are `root_shards=32` for the server default, 64 shards in soak configurations, and `gc_trim_body_soft_limit=8 MiB`; the 96 KiB experiment could not constrain the cursor-age-bound journal tail, while the 256-event count gate remains the effective trimmer. Additionally, After weighing the clamp-attribution findings, the CAS `root_shards` default was raised from 8 back to 32 (the queue mechanism had already removed the contention argument for fewer shards; 32 shards yields a ~25 KB healthy journal tail with ~1.4x batching and 4x discovery-key fan-out), soak configs were raised to 64 shards for extra `rustfs#3231` margin, and `gc_trim_body_soft_limit` was restored from the 96 KiB experiment back to an 8 MiB backstop because the trim cap cannot bind body size at all — body size is cursor-age-bound (round-cadence-bound), not trim-bound, and the working trimmer is the 256-event count gate.
The equal 30-second S3 request timeout and mount lease TTL provide no operational timeout margin for protocol-significant writes.

Review finding №22 is real: `gc_interval_sec=0` causes back-to-back GC rounds, while `gc_shards=0` makes `gc/state` unreadable and can trigger modulo-by-zero, permanently wedging GC. Additionally, The CAS review triage confirmed that zero-valued `gc_interval_sec` or `gc_shards` could cause a spin or permanent wedge; task T4 added bounds validation in commit `4fdbb3eaf11`. Additionally, `gc_interval_sec=0` can spin the scheduler and `gc_shards=0` can persist unreadable `gcs=0` state because bounds are not validated before opening the pool. Additionally, The GC configuration factory must reject `gc_interval_sec=0` and `gc_shards=0` before pool open, and `encodeGcState` must raise a runtime exception rather than rely on a release-inert `chassert`.; Unknown content-addressed disk settings are rejected; `gc_enabled` defaults to `true`, `gc_interval_sec` defaults to 60 seconds, and `gc_shards` defaults to 1. Additionally, `gc_interval_sec` and `gc_shards` must both be at least 1; zero values must fail with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` before opening a content-addressed pool. Additionally, `gc_enabled` defaults to `true`, and `gc_interval_sec` defaults to 60 seconds with a minimum value of 1 second.
